name: Training Intensity
description: Choose a useful pace for BJJ practice by agreeing on resistance, speed, and goals with your partner, then adjusting the round when the task breaks down.
summary: Choose training intensity by the job of the round: learning a movement, solving a position, or rehearsing a match.
overview: A partner can resist strongly while moving slowly, or move quickly without trying to stop you. Agree on what each person will do before relying on a vague request to go light.
key_takeaways: Separate speed, resistance, and available attacks. Change one at a time when you are trying to understand a problem.
For a new movement, start with a partner who allows the setup; then give them a specific way to resist.
Describe the round in actions: defend the pass, keep the same starting grips, or reset after a sweep.
Competition practice needs an agreed ruleset and pace. It does not require every training round to feel like a match.
Pause and renegotiate if either partner cannot follow the task or control the exchange.

bjj_applications.scenario: A pass works in drilling and falls apart as soon as your partner resists.
bjj_applications.application: Keep the starting position fixed. Ask your partner to recover their knee, without adding grips or counterattacks yet. Work on that problem before opening the round.
bjj_applications.outcome: You can identify the missing control instead of attributing every failure to a lack of effort.

bjj_applications.scenario: You asked for a light round, but your partner keeps accelerating through escapes.
bjj_applications.application: Stop briefly and make the request concrete: slow transitions, no explosive escapes, and a reset when either person loses control of the pace.
bjj_applications.outcome: Both people now have an observable agreement to follow.

bjj_applications.scenario: You want to prepare for a match.
bjj_applications.application: With your coach and a willing partner, use the event duration and rules, keep score, and agree which starts or exchanges you will rehearse. Review the decisions as well as the result.
bjj_applications.outcome: The round tests your plan under match constraints without turning the whole session into a competition.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling every difficult round a fitness problem.
common_mistakes.consequence: You may overlook prolonged squeezing, an unfamiliar position, or a pace mismatch.
common_mistakes.correction: Describe where the task broke down before choosing what to change.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a percentage such as 80% as the whole agreement.
common_mistakes.consequence: Partners can attach very different behavior to the same number.
common_mistakes.correction: Name the allowed resistance, pace, and reset condition.

common_mistakes.mistake: Increasing speed to rescue a movement you cannot yet coordinate.
common_mistakes.consequence: The failed repetitions become harder to inspect.
common_mistakes.correction: Slow the exchange, find the missing connection, and add resistance again.

training_exercises.name: One new obstacle
training_exercises.description: Start in half guard top with a familiar pass. First rehearse the setup cooperatively; then let the bottom partner try only to recover their knee shield. Reset after a pass or a recovered shield. Add another defensive option only when both partners can describe what changed.
training_exercises.focus: Adjust resistance without changing the entire problem.

training_exercises.name: Agree, roll, review
training_exercises.description: Before a positional round, each partner states a goal and the allowed pace. Start from that position and reset after a pass, sweep, or submission. Stop immediately on a tap or request to pause. After the round, compare whether the actual pace matched the agreement.

knowledge_assessment.question: How can a slow round still be difficult?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The partner can deny your grips, keep their balance, and defend the position without moving at maximum speed.
